# On the Particular Magic of Getting Lost

There's a peculiar kind of freedom that arrives when you admit you have no idea where you are. I discovered this recently while wandering through the narrow streets of a city I'd visited before but never actually explored. I had meant to find the cathedral. Instead, I found something I hadn't been looking for at all.

This is perhaps the only honest thing I can say about getting lost: it reveals something true about the difference between navigation and discovery. One is about arrival. The other is about transformation.

I think about the maps in my phone, those glowing digital guides that have made it nearly impossible to be genuinely lost anymore. There's an app-based comfort in knowing exactly where you are at all times, in having your position marked by a blue dot surrounded by all the turns you might take. But this comfort has a cost. It's the cost of the unexpected. It's the price of genuine surprise, which has become increasingly rare in a world where algorithmic recommendations predict what you might want before you know you want it.

My parents' generation—or at least, the romantic version of my parents' generation that I imagine—could still get lost. They could take a wrong turn and spend an afternoon in a neighborhood they weren't supposed to find. They could end up at a restaurant because they were hungry and it was there, not because it had four-point-three stars on a database. There's something poignant about this, something we've traded away without fully considering what we lost in the bargain.

But this essay isn't really about getting lost in the physical sense, though that's where I'll start. It's about the various ways we lose our way through life, and whether that's actually as catastrophic as we've been taught to believe.

Consider how much of our educational system is built around not getting lost. We follow curricula. We check boxes. We're told that there are right answers, correct paths, optimal trajectories. The gifted program, the Advanced Placement track, the prestigious university, the lucrative career—these are the breadcrumbs that trail toward a successful life. Deviate from the path, and you might end up... well, somewhere undefined. Somewhere off-script.

The anxiety around this is palpable in any group of teenagers. Parents ask themselves: Is my child on track? Is she behind? Will she get into a good college? Will he be able to afford a house? The trajectory is what matters. The waypoints are predetermined. Getting lost is failure.

And yet. And yet.

Some of the most interesting people I know are people who got thoroughly, completely lost at some point in their lives, and had the courage—or perhaps the desperation—to keep walking in whatever direction they found themselves heading. They're not necessarily more successful in conventional terms. But they have something else. They have a kind of authenticity that can't be manufactured or faked. They've actually lived their lives rather than merely executing them.

I know a woman who was supposed to be a lawyer. She did well in school, took the right classes, went to the right college. For three years she practiced corporate law. Then one day she realized she couldn't do it anymore. Not because she'd discovered a passion for something else—not immediately, anyway. But because she'd woken up one morning and not recognized the person staring back at her in the mirror. She was lost, and she knew it. So she quit.

What came next was messy. Years of uncertainty, of false starts, of work that paid poorly and satisfied partially. But eventually—I'm not sure she'd claim there was an "eventually," actually. Eventually is for people who follow trajectories. For her, it was more like a gradual waking up. She became a therapist. She volunteers with at-risk youth. She writes poetry that almost nobody reads but that apparently matters deeply to her. Is this a success story? By conventional metrics, certainly not. By any other metric you might devise, almost certainly yes.

The thing about being lost is that it requires a kind of humility. You have to admit that you don't know. You have to be uncertain. Our culture doesn't prize these qualities. We like confidence, decisiveness, the appearance of control. We like people who know where they're going. But there's a kind of arrogance baked into that certainty, an assumption that the map you've been given is accurate, that the destination is worth reaching, that the route has already been optimized.

What if it hasn't? What if the map is outdated? What if the destination isn't actually what you want?

I've been thinking a lot lately about the concept of "wayfinding"—a term that navigation researchers use to describe how people actually move through spaces, as opposed to how maps suggest they should. Wayfinding is improvisational. It uses landmarks rather than coordinates. It's based on noticing, on experience, on small corrections made in real time. A wayfinder doesn't follow a predetermined path so much as respond to the environment as it reveals itself.

This is actually how humans navigated for hundreds of thousands of years, before maps existed. Before GPS. Before we had the technology to pretend we could see the entire world from above, from some kind of omniscient vantage point. For most of human history, getting somewhere meant paying attention. It meant being present. It meant being prepared to be surprised.

There's a metaphor here that I'm circling around but perhaps haven't quite caught yet. Let me try again.

I think about decision-making a lot. We're taught that good decisions are made with full information, with careful deliberation, with an eye toward optimal outcomes. We're supposed to compare options, weigh pros and cons, calculate probabilities. This is the rational model of decision-making, and it dominates how we think about major life choices. But here's what I've noticed: the decisions that have mattered most in my own life were rarely made this way. Usually they were made in a moment of clarity or confusion that couldn't be reduced to a spreadsheet. Usually they involved a leap of faith, a gut feeling, an inability to see clearly where the path led but a decision to walk it anyway.

Maybe this is just me being irrational. Probably some cognitive scientist could explain that I'm engaging in motivated reasoning and confirmation bias. And they wouldn't be wrong. But I also think there's something the purely rational model misses. It misses the ways that the future is genuinely unknowable, the ways that we can't actually see the full consequences of our choices, the ways that sometimes the best decision isn't the one that optimizes a measurable outcome but the one that aligns with who you are or who you're trying to become.

I've noticed that people who are the most certain about their life paths are often people who've never had to genuinely reconsider them. They were lucky enough or privileged enough or prescient enough to choose correctly the first time. Everyone else—and I think this is most people—is engaged in this ongoing process of being lost and finding themselves and being lost again. We're wayfinding. We're paying attention to landmarks. We're making small corrections. We're noticing where the actual terrain differs from the map we were given.

Here's what I want to say clearly: being lost is not a failure of navigation. It's a fact of being human. It's not something to be ashamed of. It's not necessarily something to be fixed as quickly as possible.

This doesn't mean that everything is acceptable, that all paths are equally valid, that there's no such thing as a wise or foolish choice. That's not what I'm arguing. I'm arguing for something more subtle: that there's a difference between having a direction and having a predetermined destination. There's a difference between moving with intention and moving according to a plan someone else drew up. There's a difference between being lost and being awake.

I've been thinking about what we might call "productive lostness"—the state of being genuinely unsure about where you are or where you're going, but remaining engaged anyway. This is different from aimlessness. An aimless person has given up. A productively lost person is paying attention. They're trying things. They're willing to be surprised. They're looking for landmarks.

The city I mentioned at the beginning—I did eventually find the cathedral, but not until after I'd wandered for hours through neighborhoods I didn't know existed. I ate lunch at a small restaurant tucked into an alley, where the owner knew half the people who came in and greeted them by name. I found a bookstore that specialized in old maps, and talked to the woman who ran it for an hour about what it means to navigate. I watched a child learn to skateboard in a courtyard while his grandmother watched from a bench. These moments wouldn't have existed if I'd simply looked up the cathedral on my phone and followed the blue line.

The cathedral, when I finally found it, was beautiful. But I'm not sure it was any more beautiful than what I'd already found. The difference is that the cathedral was what I was looking for, and everything else was what I wasn't. And I think we spend so much of our lives looking for what we're supposed to want that we miss what's actually in front of us.

One more thought, and then I'll try to wrap this up.

There's a kind of conversation that I've started having more often with friends and colleagues, and it goes something like this: What would you do if you weren't afraid? What would you pursue if you knew you couldn't fail? What path would you choose if you weren't constrained by what you're supposed to want?

The difficulty of answering these questions honestly is remarkable. Most of us have internalized the voice that says: there is a right path. There is a correct destination. If you deviate, you will be lost. And being lost is dangerous.

But I wonder. I wonder whether the real danger isn't being lost, but being so certain of your direction that you stop paying attention to where you actually are. I wonder whether the greatest tragedy isn't the detours and wrong turns, but the failure to notice the landmarks along the way because you're too focused on the GPS.

I don't have a tidy conclusion here. I can't wrap this up in a bow and present you with a clear life lesson. If I'm being honest, I'm still figuring this out myself. I still feel the pull toward certainty, toward knowing where I'm going, toward believing that there's an optimal path if I can just be smart enough or disciplined enough to find it. And sometimes that pull wins out, and I spend a week or a month executing a plan, following a trajectory, trying to be where I'm supposed to be.

But increasingly, I'm trying to give myself permission to be lost. Not recklessly. Not without intention. But with openness. With the willingness to notice. With the commitment to pay attention to the actual landscape rather than the map.

And I think if more of us could do this—if we could ease up on the certainty and allow for some productive lostness—we might find that the wandering itself is the destination. That the getting lost and the finding our way is not something that happens on the way to the real life, but is actually the real life itself.
